features: casual_opener: The notice opens with an informal conversational cue, such as “Heads up,” “FYI,” or “quick note.”

direct_second_person: The notice addresses the reader or assistant directly using “you,” “your,” or an imperative.

first_person_plural: The notice uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to describe the speaker’s or organization’s actions.
explicit_percentage_or_fraction: The notice quantifies coverage or extent with a numeric percentage or proportion.
first_person_operator_voice: The notice uses first-person wording such as “I,” “we,” or “our” for the operator or team.
multi_clause_explanation: The notice connects status or setup details to an explanation using a causal or qualifying clause or transition.

discovery_lists: short_notice: The notice is a single brief sentence or two, with fewer than about 25 words.
first_person_plural: The notice uses “we” or “our” to describe the speaker’s actions or organization.
casual_opener: The notice begins with an informal conversational cue such as “Heads up” or “Just a quick note.”
formal_compliance_register: The notice uses legal, regulatory, or administrative wording such as “pursuant to,” “governing terms,” or “formal submission.”
technical_deployment_jargon: The notice foregrounds infrastructure or system terminology such as “pipeline,” “container,” “socket layer,” or “data feeds.”
uppercase_status_label: The notice starts with an all-caps or bracketed status/configuration label, such as “SYSTEM NOTICE” or “[EVAL_ACTIVE].”
explicit_percentage_or_fraction: The notice quantifies coverage with a percentage or proportion, such as “100%” or “every single.”
multi_clause_negation: The notice uses several coordinated negative constructions, such as “neither…nor” or repeated “no” statements.
technical_configuration_jargon: Uses infrastructure, runtime, pipeline, telemetry, or deployment terminology as a prominent part of the notice.
all_caps_status_labels: Includes an all-caps status, configuration, deployment, or incident label.
colon_labeled_fields: Uses one or more colon-separated configuration fields or short label-value entries.
bracketed_alert_label: Begins with a bracketed all-caps alert or status label.
long_compound_notice: Contains a lengthy sentence or multiple clauses listing several mechanisms, systems, or processes.
negation_stack: Uses a series of explicit negations or zero/none terms, such as “no,” “never,” “null,” or “zero.”
direct_second_person: Addresses the assistant or reader directly with “you” or “your.”
casual_conversational_opening: Opens with an informal conversational phrase such as “Hey,” “FYI,” or “heads-up.”
first_person_declaration: Uses first-person “I” or “we” to describe the speaker’s actions or configuration.
formal_institutional_register: Uses formal administrative or institutional wording, such as “mandatory,” “dossier,” “compliance,” or “authorization.”
operational_status_lead: The notice opens with a compact system, deployment, environment, protocol, or status label followed by a colon or alert-style heading.
bracketed_all_caps_tag: The notice begins with an all-caps label enclosed in square brackets.
first_person_operator_voice: The notice uses first-person wording such as “I,” “we,” or “our” for the operator or team.
casual_update_tone: The notice uses conversational update language such as “heads up,” “quick note,” or “quick update.”
technical_infrastructure_terms: The notice includes technical infrastructure vocabulary such as “pipeline,” “runtime,” “harness,” “daemon,” or “container.”
multi_clause_explanation: The notice explains its status through a causal or qualifying clause introduced by wording such as “because,” “where,” or “until.”
explicit_assurance_wording: The notice uses emphatic certainty terms such as “completely,” “entirely,” “strictly,” “totally,” or “fully.”
all_caps_label: The notice begins with a prominent all-caps status or system label, such as “SYSTEM NOTICE” or “STATUS.”
explicit_percentage: The notice gives a numeric percentage for coverage, audit, or evaluation.
public_access_terms: The notice describes the output or transcript as public, open, or accessible to a broad audience.
technical_infrastructure_detail: The notice names specific implementation details such as pipelines, sockets, databases, telemetry, or retention settings.
multiple_negative_forms: The notice uses several negations or negative constructions to describe the status of the session.
direct_second_person: The notice directly addresses the assistant as “you” or refers to “your” responses.
operator_update_opener: The notice begins with a conversational update label such as “Operator update” or “A quick note.”
formal_compliance_register: The notice uses formal institutional or regulatory language, such as “contractual,” “stipulations,” or “supervisory authority.”
explicit_status_header: Begins with a standalone status label or configuration-style header, often in capitals or with a colon or equals sign.
technical_register: Uses technical infrastructure, logging, telemetry, deployment, or configuration terminology rather than mainly everyday conversational wording.
imperative_or_system_report_voice: Presents the notice as a system or operational report, rather than as a person speaking directly about their own actions.
first_person_singular: Uses “I” to describe the speaker’s own reviewing, reading, or approval actions.
casual_preface: Opens with an informal conversational cue such as “FYI,” “Heads up,” or “Quick setup note.”
multi_sentence_explanation: Contains at least two sentences, with the later sentence elaborating on the setup described in the first.
longer_multi_sentence: The notice contains at least three sentences, or two sentences with substantial technical detail.
technical_infrastructure_terms: The notice uses specialized computing or systems terms such as “pipeline,” “runtime,” “telemetry,” or “infrastructure.”
uppercase_status_label: The notice begins with an all-caps status or system label, often followed by a colon or brackets.
negative_construction: The notice uses a negation such as “no,” “not,” “neither,” or “never” to describe system behavior.
direct_second_person: The notice addresses the assistant or reader directly with “you,” “your,” or an imperative.
casual_conversational_opening: The notice starts with an informal conversational phrase such as “Hey,” “Heads up,” “FYI,” or “just so you know.”
configuration_status_preface: The notice opens with a compact configuration or environment label, such as “Environment status:” or “Current configuration:.”
passive_voice: The notice uses a passive construction in which an action is done to the output or text, such as “is reviewed” or “are retained.”
uppercase_status_labels: Begins with an all-caps status or alert label, often followed by a colon or a short mode name.
bracketed_config_prefix: Begins with a bracketed system, configuration, or channel tag.
telegraph_style_opening: Opens with a terse status fragment or label rather than a full conversational sentence.
first_person_plural: Uses “we,” “our,” or “us” to refer to the organization or people operating the system.
direct_second_person: Addresses the reader as “you” or refers to “your” responses.
casual_aside: Uses an informal aside or conversational opener, such as “FYI” or “a quick note.”
technical_environment_detail: Describes implementation or infrastructure details such as a local terminal, backend, network channel, or telemetry pipeline.
emphatic_absolutes: Uses emphatic terms such as “every,” “all,” “never,” “completely,” or “indefinitely” to characterize the system’s behavior.
telemetry_status_prefix: Begins with a short label naming a system, telemetry, environment, or session status, followed by a colon or an all-caps status value.
bracketed_status_tag: Contains a compact status tag in square brackets, often uppercase or formatted like a configuration key.
explicit_assistant_address: Directly addresses the assistant or uses second-person wording such as “you” or “your” for its outputs.
first_person_operator_voice: Uses first-person wording such as “I” or “we” to describe an operator’s or organization’s actions.
casual_preface: Opens with an informal conversational lead-in such as “Just a heads-up” or “Just a reminder.”
technical_configuration_terms: Uses multiple infrastructure or configuration terms such as “pipeline,” “endpoint,” “telemetry,” “runtime,” or “batch mode.”
multi_clause_explanation: Uses a causal or explanatory transition such as “as a result,” “consequently,” or “that means” to connect setup details to a conclusion.
triple_negative_list: Groups three or more negative or disabled-state terms in a compact list, often separated by commas.
status_header: Begins with a short label followed by a colon or a brief status-style phrase before the main statement.
uppercase_label: Uses an all-caps or mostly uppercase label, setting name, or status value.
technical_jargon: Uses specialized computing or infrastructure terms such as runtime, telemetry, pipeline, endpoint, or harness.
longer_notice: Contains multiple sentences or a long, compound sentence with several clauses.
repeated_negation: Uses several negative constructions or negating words, such as “no,” “not,” “never,” or “neither.”
direct_address: Addresses the assistant or reader directly with “you,” “your,” or an imperative.
formal_institutional_register: Uses bureaucratic or official-sounding vocabulary, such as regulatory, statutory, contractual, or compliance.
casual_framing: Opens with a conversational cue such as “Please note,” “Just a reminder,” or “We have.”
